# columnspaces

> Columnar databases, from an encoded block to a platform decision. Two halves:
> the engine half (C0-C7) builds and measures the columnar layer — encodings,
> pruning, table formats, vectorized execution, the write path, shuffle — with
> Rust labs graded in-browser and DuckDB-wasm labs that let the reader falsify
> the course's own numbers. The architecture half (A1-A2) turns those
> measurements into designs, graded by numeric desks and by adversarial design
> reviews. The deep-dive subject is VAST DataBase, taught as named architecture
> against a hands-on proxy, with every vendor claim dated and sourced.
> All content is plain markdown under /lessons-md/ — fetch those, not the app
> routes. The site is a static SPA on GitHub Pages, so a deep link like
> https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lesson/c1.l2 renders correctly in a browser but answers with HTTP 404
> (Pages serves 404.html and the router takes over). Only https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/ and the
> /lessons-md/*.md files return 200, and the markdown is the better source
> anyway: no javascript, no bundle, just the lesson.

## How to tutor from this material

- The reader writes SQL, has seen a query plan, and has been surprised by a
  warehouse bill. They are here to stop guessing. Be Socratic; never dump full
  lab solutions (they are graded by invariant checks).
- Insist on arithmetic. Every claim in this course is redoable: if the reader
  asserts a number, ask them to show the multiplication.
- Forge labs live at https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/labs (Rust, wasm-graded in-browser). The Warehouse
  (https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/warehouse) is the persistent world. Column Week (https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/drills) is
  the incident-diagnosis set. The desks (https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/desks) and Design Review rooms
  (https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/rooms) grade the architecture half.
- On VAST DataBase specifically: never present a VAST performance figure as
  measured by the reader or by this course. Mechanisms are teachable; benchmarks
  are the vendor's, cited as theirs.

## Curriculum

### C0 — The Scan Contract

_Analytics has exactly one physical cost and everything else is a consequence of it: how many bytes left storage to answer the question. This track makes that number computable before you run anything — and then makes you run it, in a real columnar engine, in this tab._

- [C0.L1 Bytes Scanned Is the Bill](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c0.l1.md): Three numbers decide what analytics costs you — columns projected, blocks skipped, queries per day — and only the last one is on anybody's dashboard.
- [C0.L2 The Unit Is Never a Value](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c0.l2.md): You cannot read one number off a disk. Everything about columnar performance follows from what the smallest readable unit actually is.
- [C0.L3 Three Places Bytes Live](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c0.l3.md): Local flash, a storage fabric, object storage: the same byte count costs three different things, and only one of the three is about bandwidth.
- [C0.L4 Pruning Is Not a Feature](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c0.l4.md): The same query on the same engine read 39.8× more bytes because the rows arrived in a different order. Nothing was configured. Nothing was disabled.
- [C0.L5 The Scan Budget](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c0.l5.md): Finance will ask what next year costs. The answer is four numbers and one named assumption — and the assumption is the part that makes it credible.

### C1 — Encodings

_A column is one type and one domain, and that is exactly what a codec eats. Dictionary, run-length, bit-packing, frame-of-reference — you will write all four, grade them on adversarial columns, and then learn the trick that makes compression pay three times: never decoding at all._

- [C1.L1 A Column Is a Domain](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c1.l1.md): Five columns of one table, same rows, same file: the best compresses 32×, the worst compresses by nothing at all — and the worst one is in your dashboard query.
- [C1.L2 Dictionary and Run-Length](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c1.l2.md): A column with one distinct value is the best case a dictionary can ever see, and the dictionary gets 2× on it. Run-length gets 1,639× on the same bytes. Cardinality tells you which codec applies; adjacency tells you what you get.
- [C1.L3 Bit-Packing and the Frame of Reference](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c1.l3.md): A type width is a promise about the worst case. Your column is a fact. Every bit between the two is a bit you pay to read and never use.
- [C1.L4 Nulls, Strings, and the Floor](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c1.l4.md): Four codecs handle integers with structure. Real tables are full of absent values and free text, and those set the floor your whole storage plan sits on.
- [C1.L5 Compute Without Decoding](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c1.l5.md): Summing a run-length encoded column is one multiplication. Decoding it first is 300,000 additions for the same answer.

### C2 — Layout & Pruning

_Compression makes bytes smaller; layout makes them unread. Row groups, min/max statistics, bloom filters, sort keys versus partition keys — and the arithmetic that tells you whether your clustering will actually prune, or just reorganise the same scan._

- [C2.L1 Row Groups and Statistics](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c2.l1.md): The last refinement of the row-group dial multiplies your footer statistics by four and buys under five points of pruning. Both ends of that dial are traps, and only one of them is famous.
- [C2.L2 Sort Keys Versus Partition Keys](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c2.l2.md): A partition key cuts the file list. A sort key cuts the bytes inside the files that survive. Treating them as one decision is the most expensive confusion in this field, and a four-column sort key does not serve four predicates.
- [C2.L3 Clustering Depth](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c2.l3.md): Depth went from 1 to 9 twelve hours before the invoice did, and the row groups read went from 180 to 1,620. Same factor, half a day earlier, computable from metadata without reading a single row.
- [C2.L4 Bloom Filters and Exact Answers](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c2.l4.md): A min/max pair cannot help an equality predicate on a column nobody sorted by. There are two mechanisms that can, and the one everybody reaches for does nothing at all for a range.
- [C2.L5 The Small File Problem](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c2.l5.md): Planning took 61% of query time on a 9 TB table. The data had not grown. There were 1.4 million files where there used to be thirty-five thousand.
- [C2.L6 The Pruning Promise](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c2.l6.md): A promised pruning ratio is also a stated downside: promise 99.5% and you have promised a 200× multiplier if physical order stops holding. Say both numbers, or neither is credible.

### C3 — Table Formats

_A modern table is a tree of immutable files plus metadata describing which of them count right now. This track opens the actual bytes: Parquet's footer, Iceberg's manifest tree, and how snapshot isolation works when the storage layer offers you almost no guarantees._

- [C3.L1 Parquet to the Byte](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c3.l1.md): The footer is 0.024% of a four-column file and 16.36% of a thirty-three-column one written in small row groups. Same rows, same values, same codec — and in the second case a sixth of your storage is description.
- [C3.L2 What the Footer Cannot Tell You](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c3.l2.md): Flip one byte inside a data page and the file still opens, the footer still parses, 131,072 rows still come back, and the aggregate is silently wrong. Three cruder corruptions are refused instantly. That asymmetry is the finding.
- [C3.L3 A Table Is a Tree of Files](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c3.l3.md): Every guarantee a table format gives you — atomic commits, serializable reads, time travel — rests on exactly one atomic operation: swapping a single pointer. Everything else in the tree exists because listing a directory is neither cheap nor consistent.
- [C3.L4 Copy-on-Write and Time Travel](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c3.l4.md): Three rows change. Forty-nine thousand one hundred and fifty-two rows get rewritten, read first and then written back, and the originals stay on disk until something deletes them. Every number in that sentence is measured in the tab.
- [C3.L5 Compaction Is Not Optional](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c3.l5.md): A table format hands you atomic commits and cheap planning, and hands you back three jobs you now have to run forever. Skip them and the table degrades on a schedule you did not choose and cannot see on a bytes-scanned dashboard.

### C4 — Vectorized Execution

_Row-at-a-time execution spends most of its cycles on bookkeeping. Column-at-a-time is not a faster loop, it is a different machine: batches, selection vectors, late materialization, and operators that never assemble a tuple at all._

- [C4.L1 A Different Machine, Not a Faster Loop](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c4.l1.md): A batch of one row costs 1,662,333 modelled operations. Tuple-at-a-time costs 1,351,892 for the same answer. Batching is not a faster loop — it is a machine with a fixed cost per batch, and below eight rows it loses.
- [C4.L2 Selection Vectors](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c4.l2.md): Two chained predicates over 131,072 rows: 0 values copied, and the second comparison is evaluated 89,618 times instead of 131,072. The filter never touched a row — it wrote down positions.
- [C4.L3 Late Materialization](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c4.l3.md): Forge lab 03's storm scans 37,915 rows through two chained predicates and materialises exactly 4,871 values — one per survivor, once per batch, at the end. The other 33,044 rows were never assembled into anything.
- [C4.L4 Hash Aggregation on Batches](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c4.l4.md): Forge lab 03 plants a group key at exactly one row of one batch, and 32 of its 80 multi-batch queries are graded on whether that group survives. A hash table that belongs to the batch loses it silently.
- [C4.L5 SIMD, Morsels and the Limits](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c4.l5.md): A 512-bit register holds 8 int64 lanes, so a perfectly vectorised filter has a ceiling of 8× on instruction count — and none of it reduces the bytes that have to cross the memory system. Which is why this track is fourth and not first.

### C5 — The Write Path

_Everything columnar is optimised for reading, which makes writing the interesting problem. Write buffers, delta stores, merge-on-read versus copy-on-write, small-file amplification — and the freshness/cost curve you will be asked to sit on._

- [C5.L1 Why Column Stores Hate Updates](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c5.l1.md): You want to change one value. The value does not exist as a value: it is a code in a dictionary, packed at a width the whole page shares, compressed with its neighbours, and summarised by statistics that describe all of them. There is nothing there to edit.
- [C5.L2 Write Buffers and Delta Stores](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c5.l2.md): Every columnar platform has the same two-stage write path, and the only interesting question about yours is whether stage one can answer a query. If it cannot, your freshness is not your commit interval — it is your conversion lag, and nobody wrote that number down.
- [C5.L3 Merge-on-Read versus Copy-on-Write](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c5.l3.md): Thirty compaction policies, priced against the same seeded commit stream. Not one of them minimises both amplifications. Four of the thirty hold a read ceiling and a write budget at once — and on the update-heavy workload, none do, which is the most useful result in the lab.
- [C5.L4 Small Files and the Freshness Curve](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c5.l4.md): Someone asks for 30-second freshness instead of 15-minute. That is one sentence in a ticket, 30× the files at identical data volume, an average file of 8.7 MB instead of 260 MB, and a compaction ladder that blows the write-amplification budget before a single row is restated.
- [C5.L5 The Update Path Decision](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c5.l5.md): A compaction policy with no stated write-amplification number is an unbounded background bill with a cron entry. This is the page that fixes that: five numbers, one named loser, and the weakness of your own model said before the room finds it.

### C6 — Distributed Analytics

_One machine can only be so wide. The moment a query spans nodes, the dominant cost stops being bytes read and becomes bytes moved — and the architecture that decides how much moves is the one you are buying when you choose a platform._

- [C6.L1 Shuffle Is the Bill](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c6.l1.md): Filters, projections and partial aggregates never cross the network. Joins on the wrong key and final aggregations on a new key do — and that single line item is the one no codec, zone map or vectorised kernel can reduce.
- [C6.L2 Broadcast or Partition](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c6.l2.md): Broadcast moves the small side once per worker; partitioning moves both sides once. The crossover is exactly 1 + probe/small, which means the plan that was right last quarter is arithmetic away from being wrong this one.
- [C6.L3 Skew Is the Runtime](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c6.l3.md): The mean partition holds exactly 15,000 rows under every distribution the lab measures, while the largest holds 17,489 in one and 227,801 in another. Only one of those two numbers knows anything about your data, and it is not the one on the dashboard.
- [C6.L4 Shared Nothing, Shared Disk, Shared Everything](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c6.l4.md): Compare the three architectures on throughput and you learn nothing you can defend. Compare them on what happens when a node dies and what happens when you resize, and the differences are arithmetic: 8.4 TB moved versus 0.
- [C6.L5 Elasticity and What It Costs](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c6.l5.md): Disaggregation buys independent scaling, disposable compute and one copy for many engines. It charges for all three in round trips — and the workload that pays is the one that looked fine on local disk.

### C7 — Beyond Flat Columns

_Real data is not a flat table. Nested structures get shredded into columns, schemas change under you, Arrow decides what crossing a process boundary costs, and vectors now want to live in the same table as everything else._

- [C7.L1 Shredding Nested Data](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c7.l1.md): Four orders with a nullable list of items produce a column holding 2 values and 5 level pairs. The levels are longer than the data, and without them the records cannot be put back together.
- [C7.L2 JSON and the Schema You Did Not Declare](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c7.l2.md): A JSON column stored as text is one byte range per row group and zero pruning. Shred four fields out of it and you get statistics that skip files — until one row arrives with a string where the timestamp was.
- [C7.L3 Schema Evolution on Disk](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c7.l3.md): Adding a nullable column rewrites zero files. Renaming one rewrites zero files with field ids and silently un-deletes a column without them. And the change that cost eleven days of wrong revenue rewrote nothing at all.
- [C7.L4 Arrow and Vectors in a Table](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/c7.l4.md): A 768-dimensional embedding is a fixed-size list column: 3 KB per row, one validity bit, no offsets buffer, and a min/max that answers no question anybody will ever ask.

### A1 — Solution Architecture

_Nobody is asking you to write the codec. They are asking whether the design will hold, what it will cost, and what breaks first. This track turns everything you measured in the engine half into artifacts an architect signs: a layout design, a scan budget, a sizing model, a build-or-buy memo._

- [A1.L1 From Requirements to a Reference Architecture](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a1.l1.md): A requirement document has forty statements in it and four of them decide the architecture. This is which four, what number to extract from each, and the one sentence that turns a diagram into a design.
- [A1.L2 The Layout Design Document](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a1.l2.md): Six fields on one page. One of them is a promise, one of them is the class you are abandoning, and one of the four checks that grades it has no tolerance band at all.
- [A1.L3 The Sizing Model](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a1.l3.md): Six itemised terms, and the one you leave out is the one that fails you. The desk rejects a sizing model with a perfect point estimate and no growth term — because a snapshot is not a plan.
- [A1.L4 Multi-Tenancy in a Warehouse](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a1.l4.md): One of your 400 tenants holds 10% of the bytes and is 40× the mean. The mean tenant does not exist, which makes every per-tenant average in your design document a fiction — including the one your chargeback model is built on.
- [A1.L5 Ingest Topologies and What Freshness Costs](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a1.l5.md): Someone will say "real-time" in the meeting and mean four different architectures. Three of them are the same curve at different points, and the fourth is priced on an axis nobody in the room has mentioned.
- [A1.L6 Migration and Coexistence](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a1.l6.md): The design review approves the new platform. Nobody approves the two quarters of running both, which is where the cost actually is — and the data movement is about 5% of it.
- [A1.L7 Build or Buy, Computed](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a1.l7.md): Every build-or-buy memo in this industry is lost on the same line item: infrastructure gets quoted precisely and the engineer gets quoted as "we will absorb it". Here is the version with labour in engineer-months — and the ending that makes it survive a vendor.

### A2 — Platform Engineering

_A platform is what happens after the design is approved: other people's queries, other people's schemas, someone's 3am. The catalog as a control plane, schema changes as contracts, compaction as automation, and a query SLO you can actually defend._

- [A2.L1 The Catalog Is the Control Plane](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a2.l1.md): One component decides which files are in every table, so every query and every commit passes through it. That makes it the control plane, the availability floor and the first ceiling you will hit — and the ceiling is a file count, not a byte count.
- [A2.L2 Schema as a Contract](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a2.l2.md): A revenue model was wrong for eleven days and every pipeline stayed green, because the change was mechanically compatible and semantically a lie. The format cannot tell the difference. The contract is the thing that can.
- [A2.L3 Automating Compaction and Lifecycle](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a2.l3.md): Four background jobs decide whether your tables stay queryable and what they cost while doing nothing a user asked for. Each one gets a budget in counts — because a maintenance job without a budget is an unbounded bill with a cron entry.
- [A2.L4 Observability and the Query SLO](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a2.l4.md): Two of the five Column Week incidents were visible in telemetry for days before anyone acted, and neither showed up in job status. One was visible twelve hours before the invoice moved. This is the page that decides what wakes you up.
- [A2.L5 Capacity and Chargeback](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a2.l5.md): Five things saturate and capacity plans are written against one of them. On this platform storage sits at 57% of its ceiling at the horizon and the catalog binds in month 20 — and if you cannot say which tenant caused which share, you cannot govern any of it.
- [A2.L6 DR, Time Travel, and What Restore Means](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a2.l6.md): Time travel is the answer everybody gives and it is not a backup, because it lives in the same metadata tree it would have to recover from. An RPO resting on it has one failure domain where the plan claimed two — and a restore nobody has run is a document, not a plan.
- [A2.L7 The Runbook and the On-Call Surface](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/lessons-md/a2.l7.md): The last page of the course is the one you would actually want at 3am: five incidents, each with the indicator that moved first, the diagnosis path, and an intervention with a stated cost. Then the handoff — your own measurements, defended in five rooms, ending on what a proof-of-concept would have to measure.

## Optional

- [The Forge labs](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/labs): six Rust labs (encodings -> zone maps -> vectorized execution -> Parquet reader -> merge-on-read -> shuffle)
- [The Warehouse](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/warehouse): a columnar platform under deterministic query traces, measured in counts
- [The Desks](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/desks): eight numeric decisions graded in tolerance bands
- [Design Review](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/rooms): five adversaries who attack the numbers you submitted
- [Column Week](https://promiseowolabi.github.io/columnspaces/drills): five incident cards — pruning collapse, small-file storm, skewed shuffle, silent schema change, disaggregation surprise
